articles.title: Man accused of posing as 49ers player in $1.3M romance scam seen in video
articles.excerpt: A man accused of posing as a San Francisco 49ers player to scam women out of about $1.3 million appeared in a video obtained by OutKick.
articles.content:

by Kendal Lewis

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WZTV) — A man accused of posing as a San Francisco 49ers player to scam women out of about $1.3 million appeared in a video, apparently pretending to sign with the NFL team.

Authorities say 35-year-old Daejon Love used a fake NFL persona and romantic relationships to convince women to give him money for investments that did not exist.

In the video obtained by OutKick in 2024, Love appears to sign what he represented as an NFL contract.

When asked which team he was joining, Love responded, “Niners.”

However, representatives for the NFL and 49ers told investigators Love had never been employed by either organization, according to an FBI affidavit.

Investigators say Love used dating apps and social media to meet women and portrayed himself as either a 49ers player or wealthy real estate developer.

Authorities say 35-year-old Love and 18-year-old Taylor Jamie Chan, who allegedly posed as Love’s financial adviser, used fake investment accounts and promises of large returns to convince women to send money.

At least 26 women in California, Idaho, Oregon and Washington allegedly lost about $1.3 million.

Love and Chan were arrested Aug. 24 in Boise, Idaho. Both face charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud.

The FBI believes there may be additional victims.

Love and Chan are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

articles.title: From Faribault to the Fair, the Tilt-A-Whirl took its first spin 100 years ago this summer
articles.excerpt: In its first year on the Fairgrounds, in 1926, the now-iconic attraction cost 15 cents to ride.
articles.content:
In its first year on the Fairgrounds, in 1926, the now-iconic attraction cost 15 cents to ride

When the Tilt-A-Whirl debuted at the Minnesota State Fair in 1926, the same year it was invented in a Faribault backyard some 50 miles south of the Fairgrounds, each ride cost 15 cents.

Out of the 401,000 or so people who visited the eight-day State Fair that year, 4,233 took a spin on the new contraption.

Tens of thousands more have tilted and whirled over the past 100 years, and the ride remains a popular Fair staple, though it has since moved from the high-thrill Midway to the family-friendly Kidway.

In his 1926 patent application for the Tilt-A-Whirl, Faribault woodworker and craftsman Herbert Sellner fairly dispassionately described his creation as “a new and improved amusement apparatus which will furnish pleasurable and unexpected sensations.”

Growing up the son of a respected cabinet-maker, Sellner seemed to have been known as a woodshop tinkerer. His first patent, granted in 1910, was for a sandpapering machine; his second, in 1917, outlined a particular type of foldable drop-leaf table. But his first big break came in 1922, when he created a water toboggan ride — a massive slide that riders would fly down on wooden sleds, a sort of self-service log flume — that he began selling to beachfront resorts.

He had another idea in the works, a madcap merry-go-round with the unpredictable instability of a floating raft, but his early prototypes evidently didn’t manage to nail the rotational physics he envisioned. So he sat his 10 year-old son Art in a chair he’d rigged up on caster wheels, and placed chair and boy atop an oak dining table.

To the Pioneer Press in 1992, Art’s son Bruce Sellner explained what happened next: “Here’s my dad sitting on top of this — my dad’s got a Buster Brown haircut and knickers — and my grandfather and his brother are lifting up this table to send this chair around, to figure out the angles they need to make the chair spin.”

As Herbert Sellner watched his son roll around the table, the lore goes, something clicked for him. In his basement woodshop that summer of 1926, he fabricated the components of what would become the first Tilt-A-Whirl, which he assembled in a neighbor’s backyard.

Like the water toboggan ride, to put it bluntly, the first Tilt-A-Whirl was a bit crude. It consisted of nine passenger cars on wooden octopus-style arms, with rotation powered by “a cable hooked up to a tractor engine,” as a 2006 Pioneer Press retrospective noted. The now-classic rounded shell car design wouldn’t come till later; the early cars looked like the back halves of Christmas sleighs covered with fabric canopies resembling those atop four-poster beds.

And riders were immediately enamored. Seeing the ride’s success at the State Fair, the Wildwood Amusement Park, which sat at the end of a streetcar line in White Bear Lake, immediately bought Sellner’s first Tilt-A-Whirl to install for the 1927 season. The price: $4,500, equivalent to more than $87,000 today — still much less than the estimated mid-six-figure price tag of a new Tilt-A-Whirl in 2026. (Wildwood closed in the 1930s and the fate of its history-making Tilt-A-Whirl is unknown.)

Herbert Sellner died of a blood disease in 1930, at age 43. The family business continued under Art Sellner and later Bruce Sellner, who grew up accompanying his father on business trips to Midways and carnivals and took over operations in his mid-20s.

“When I was a kid, I spent more time upside down than rightside up,” Bruce Sellner told the Pioneer Press in 1992.

Separately, Art and Bruce Sellner both died in 1995. The Sellner Manufacturing Company factory continued to produce Tilt-A-Whirls in Faribault until it was sold to a Texas company in 2011.

Even though the Tilt-A-Whirl is no longer made in its hometown, the ride has undeniable staying power a century after its Minnesota State Fair debut.

“People identify with it,” Walt Wittmer, then the vice president and general manager of Valleyfair, told the Pioneer Press in 1992. “It’s a ride that dad has grown up with; now he’s a grandfather, he passes it on to the kids. It’s a three- or four-generation ride.”

articles.title: Amid Growing Galliano Backlash, Met Gala Mulls Date Change - Report
articles.excerpt: Amid backlash over the Met Gala's choice to honor designer John Galliano, officials are "mulling" whether to reschedule away from Holocaust Remembrance Day.
articles.content:
Amid growing backlash over the Met Gala‘s choice to honor designer John Galliano at the big event next May, Met trustees and board members are “mulling” whether to reschedule the fundraiser away from the previously announced May 3 date to avoid coinciding with the Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day.

The possibility of postponing the gala for a week has been raised in a New York Times report on the increasing Galliano backlash: The accomplished British fashion designer was convicted of a hate crime by a French court in 2011 for making public antisemitic outbursts, and earlier this month The Times reported that Vogue’s global editorial director and a Met trustee Anna Wintour, Galliano and other Gala organizers had been meeting over the course of the past year with “influential rabbis and Jewish leaders” in New York City “to get their thoughts on the potential issues with next year’s planned fashion extravaganza — a show dedicated to Galliano’s work — and perhaps their blessing for it.”

Now a second Times report notes that concern over the choice of honoree has only become more troublesome since that first article was published a month ago. According to an article by Vanessa Friedman, the Times’ fashion director and chief fashion critic, and Times’ Style writer Jacob Bernstein appearing today on the news site, Met trustees and board members “have been scrambling to do damage control” over the Galliano selection.

Watch on Deadline

“For starters,” Friedman and Bernstein report, “they are mulling whether to move the date of the next Met Gala from its usual slot, the first Monday in May, to the week after. In 2027, Yom HaShoah, also known as Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day, will fall on the scheduled party date.”

Met Gala officials, including trustee Anna Wintour, who is a noted champion of Galliano, have not publicly addressed the possibility of a gala date change. Vogue magazine, the de facto official publication of record for the gala, still lists, as of today, May 3 as the gala date.

Today’s Times article details the opposition to Galliano’s selection that has grown among Jewish leaders in recent days. According to the Times, “Donors have contacted Met executives and threatened to rescind gifts to the museum if the exhibition moves forward as planned. They have reached out to Wintour, Andrew Bolton, the curator of the Costume Institute, and Max Hollein, the museum’s director.”

For example, the paper notes, Julie Menin, the speaker of the City Council, and one of the most senior Jewish officials in city government, called the museum’s decision to highlight Galliano’s career “a serious mistake” in a letter she sent on Thursday to Hollein, Bolton and Wintour.

“Our cultural institutions, particularly those that receive funding from the City of New York, have a responsibility to demonstrate that hatred and bigotry carry consequences,” Menin wrote in the letter, which was shared with The New York Times by a museum official. “Words matter, and whom we choose to elevate is a direct statement of our values and what we are willing to tolerate.”

According to The Times, Menin wasn’t the only newly outspoken critic of the honoree. Arne Glimcher, described by the paper as an “art world titan,” recently sent an email critical of the plan to Hollein and David Breslin, a Met curator, stating, “I don’t think you have considered the cost of this action and its reverberations to come,” adding that he and his wife “are seriously reconsidering other works that have been earmarked from our collection to the Met in our wills.”

And Jill Kargman, a longtime member of the patron group Friends of the Costume Institute, announced she is stepping down from her role due to the Galliano project.

In a statement to the Times yesterday, museum director Hollein said, “The Met has no tolerance for antisemitism, racism or prejudice of any kind. We are in close consultation with Jewish leaders and other stakeholders, and we take the concerns we’ve heard very seriously.” He added that Met leadership “is developing a thoughtful plan for next year’s exhibition and gala that meets the moral and ethical standards set by the museum.”
